title: Mandates without means? Governance framework for forestry extension in Uganda
content:
Abstract
Decentralized forestry governance frequently transfers responsibilities to local actors without the resources needed to fulfill them. This study examines how Uganda’s framework translates into operational support for District Forestry Officers (DFOs) and why persistent implementation gaps threaten the country’s forest landscape restoration targets under the Bonn Challenge and AFR100. Drawing on Decentralization Theory and Conservation of Resources (COR) theory, the study analyses how institutional arrangements and resource conditions interact to shape frontline extension capacity. A qualitative design combined Key Informant Interviews (KIIs) (n = 20), five regional focus group discussions, and document review, with hybrid thematic coding. Findings reveal a structural “mandates without means” dynamic: formal responsibilities are devolved amid overlapping roles, limited decision space, and outdated legal instruments, while chronic shortages of staff, transport, and operational funds trigger resource loss spirals that erode motivation, field coverage, and enforcement. Political interference and weak coordination further dilute implementation. By integrating COR with decentralization analysis, the study demonstrates that unfunded mandates become self-reinforcing when resource scarcity undermines officers’ ability to act on their authority, a mechanism that single theory studies overlook. Strengthening extension performance requires bundled reform: clearer institutional boundaries, legally protected district-level decision-making, and ring-fenced operational budgets, not piecemeal increases in any one domain. These insights carry direct implications for decentralized governance systems worldwide struggling to reconcile ambitious restoration pledges with frontline realities. Without alignment, decentralization risks permanently devolving responsibility without the means to deliver, perpetuating policy failure.
